name: Maximón (Rilaj Maam)
description: Maximón, also known as Rilaj Maam ('Grandfather' or 'Great Grandfather' in K'iche'), is a syncretic deity venerated in the Guatemala highlands. He is a complex figure blending pre-Columbian Maya beliefs with Spanish colonial Catholicism. Represented as a mannequin-like effigy dressed in dark sunglasses, a suit, and a scarf, Maximón sits in brotherhood shrines (cofradías) across the western highlands. Devotees offer him cigars, rum, and money in exchange for favors — protection, health, prosperity, or even revenge. He is both feared and revered: a guardian of communities who can also bring misfortune to those who cross him.
appearance: Maximón is represented as a life-sized wooden mannequin seated in a chair. He wears a dark suit, a tie, dark sunglasses, and a patterned scarf wrapped around his neck. His face is carved wood, often painted pale. He holds a cigar or cigarette in his mouth and is adorned with bills of money tucked into his clothing. In some cofradías, he wears a wide-brimmed hat.
behavior: Maximón is said to walk at night, visiting homes and drinking establishments. He is accompanied by two invisible dogs that bark warnings. He smokes constantly and drinks rum, which devotees pour at his feet. He rewards loyalty with protection and prosperity, but punishes betrayal with illness, madness, or death. During Semana Santa (Holy Week), he is paraded through towns on a litter carried by cofradía members.
habitat: Cofradía shrines — small rooms or buildings maintained by brotherhoods in towns across the K'iche' Maya highlands, particularly in Santiago Atitlán, Sololá, and Totonicapán.
cultural_significance: Maximón is the most visible example of Maya-Catholic syncretism in Guatemala. His veneration survived centuries of colonial suppression and represents the resilience of indigenous spiritual practice. The cofradía system that maintains him is a key social institution in highland Maya communities, blending religious, political, and social functions. His image has become a symbol of Guatemalan cultural identity.
summary: Maximón (Rilaj Maam) is a syncretic Maya-Catholic deity venerated in Guatemala's highlands, represented as a mannequin in dark sunglasses and a suit, offered cigars and rum in exchange for protection.
fun_fact: During Semana Santa in Santiago Atitlán, Maximón is carried through the streets on a litter while cofradía members offer him cigars and aguardiente — the only time he leaves his shrine all year.
seo_description: Syncretic Maya-Catholic deity venerated in Guatemala's highlands, represented as a mannequin in dark sunglasses and offered cigars and rum.
source: Recinos, Adrián. 'El Quinto Inkarri: El movimiento mesiánico-festivo de los Mayas de Todo Santo Cuchumatán, Huehuetenango, Guatemala.' CEUR-USAC, 1977. Carlsen, Robert S. 'The War for the Heart of Santiago: Ritual, Power, and the Persistence of Tradition in Highland Guatemala.' University of Texas Press, 1997.

name: La Llorona
description: La Llorona — 'The Weeping Woman' — is one of the most widespread ghosts in Guatemalan folklore. She is the spirit of a woman who drowned her children in a river, either out of madness or despair, and now wanders waterways at night, weeping and searching for them. Her cries of ¡Ay, mis hijos! ('Oh, my children!') echo through the streets and along rivers after dark. In Guatemala, she is particularly associated with the shores of Lake Atitlán and the rivers of the western highlands. Parents warn children never to go near water after dark, lest La Llorona drag them beneath the surface to replace her lost children.
appearance: La Llorona appears as a tall, gaunt woman dressed in white, with long black hair covering her face. Her eyes are hollow and glowing. She wears a tattered white dress soaked with river water. Her hands are pale and skeletal. In some accounts, her face is beautiful but aged, while in others it is a decomposing skull.
behavior: She wanders along rivers, lakes, and dark streets at night, weeping loudly. She calls out for her children. If she encounters a child, she may try to lure them to the water's edge or seize them. She is most active during rainy season and near water. Some accounts say she can be heard but not seen; others describe her as a solid, dangerous presence.
habitat: Riverbanks, lake shores, and dark streets near water. Particularly associated with Lake Atitlán, the Motagua River, and colonial-era streets in Antigua Guatemala.
cultural_significance: La Llorona is one of the most important cautionary figures in Guatemalan oral tradition. Her story serves multiple social functions: warning children away from dangerous waterways, reinforcing family bonds, and encoding anxieties about motherhood and gender. She is also a figure of genuine grief — her story evokes sympathy alongside fear. Variations exist across Guatemala, with local versions adding regional details.
summary: La Llorona is the ghost of a woman who drowned her children and now wanders waterways at night, weeping and searching for them, in one of Guatemala's most widespread cautionary legends.
fun_fact: In Guatemala City, La Llorona sightings are reported near the Las Vacas River and Lake Amatitlán every rainy season — local newspapers still run 'Llorona panic' stories in July and August.
seo_title: La Llorona – The Weeping Woman of Guatemala
seo_description: The ghost of a woman who drowned her children, wandering Guatemalan waterways at night, weeping and searching for them.
source: Garona, Julio. 'Leyendas de Guatemala.' José de Pineda Ibarra, 1975. Recinos, Adrián. 'Tz'utujil: Etnología, Historia y Mitología de los Indios Tz'utujiles de Guatemala.' Tipografía Nacional de Guatemala, 1946.

name: Tzitzimimeh
description: The Tzitzimimeh (singular: Tzitzimitl) are skeletal female demons from Maya and broader Mesoamerican mythology who descend from the stars during eclipses and cosmic disorder. They are associated with darkness, death, and the devouring of human flesh. In K'iche' Maya tradition, they serve as agents of the lords of Xibalba (the underworld), emerging when the cosmic order breaks down. They are depicted as skeletal figures wearing skirts decorated with human hearts and hands. Despite their terrifying nature, they also serve as protectors of women in labor — a duality common in Mesoamerican supernatural beings.
appearance: Tzitzimimeh appear as tall, skeletal women with exposed bones and hollow eye sockets. They wear skirts adorned with hearts, hands, and severed heads. Their skin is dark or grey, and their hair hangs wild. Some accounts describe them as beautiful women who reveal their skeletal form only when attacking. They often carry obsidian knives.
behavior: They descend from the sky during eclipses, droughts, or periods of social chaos. They devour humans, particularly men, and are drawn to areas of disorder. During solar eclipses, people in Guatemala traditionally make noise — banging pots and shouting — to frighten them away. Despite their ferocity, midwives invoke their protective aspect during difficult births.
habitat: The stars and the cosmic void. They descend to earth during eclipses and periods of darkness. In folklore, they are said to lurk in caves, abandoned buildings, and the spaces between worlds.
cultural_significance: The Tzitzimimeh represent the ever-present threat of cosmic disorder in Maya belief. Their mythology encodes astronomical knowledge (solar eclipses) and social anxieties (war, famine, disease). The duality of their nature — terrifying demons yet protectors of birthing women — reflects the Maya understanding of creation and destruction as intertwined forces. They remain important in contemporary Highland Maya communities.
summary: The Tzitzimimeh are skeletal female demons from Maya mythology who descend from the stars during eclipses and cosmic disorder to devour humans, yet also protect women in labor.
fun_fact: In Guatemala, people still bang pots and scream during solar eclipses to drive away the Tzitzimimeh — a tradition that has persisted for over 500 years since the Spanish conquest.
seo_title: Tzitzimimeh – Star Demons of Maya Mythology
seo_description: Skeletal female demons from Maya mythology who descend from the stars during eclipses to devour humans.
source: Read, Kay Almere and Jason González. 'Handbook of Mesoamerican Mythology.' ABC-CLIO, 2000. Taube, Karl A. 'The Major Gods of Ancient Yucatan.' Dumbarton Oaks, 1992.

name: Witz (Mountain Spirit)
description: In K'iche' Maya cosmology, the Witz is the sacred mountain spirit — the living consciousness of the mountains themselves. Mountains are not merely geological features but animate beings with their own souls, histories, and powers. The Witz guards sacred sites, hidden caves, and the entrances to the underworld. Maya kings derived their authority from the Witz, and the word for 'throne' and 'mountain' are the same in many Maya languages. Even today, Highland Maya communities perform ceremonies at mountain peaks and cave entrances to honor the Witz and ask for rain, harvests, and protection.
appearance: The Witz is rarely depicted in human form. When manifested, it appears as the mountain itself — a vast, living stone face with eyes of water and a mouth of cave darkness. In carved stelae, it is shown as a jaguar-headed mountain with a gaping maw from which serpents emerge. In some accounts, it takes the form of an enormous jaguar or a stone giant covered in moss and vegetation.
behavior: The Witz watches over its territory silently. It accepts offerings left at cave entrances and mountain peaks — copal incense, jade, blood offerings in ancient times. It grants visions to those who enter its caves with proper ceremony. It punishes those who disrespect sacred sites with earthquakes, landslides, or madness. During the Maya creation story, the Witz was formed from the first blood sacrifice.
habitat: Mountain peaks, sacred caves, and volcanic highlands throughout Guatemala. Particularly associated with Tajumalco, the Cuchumatanes, and the volcanic chain around Lake Atitlán.
cultural_significance: The Witz is central to Maya understanding of the cosmos. Mountains are the axis mundi — the connection between the underworld (Xibalba), the middle world (earth), and the heavens. The Witz concept explains why Maya cities were built around sacred mountains and why caves were the most important ritual sites. Contemporary Maya communities still maintain sacred mountain sites and perform ceremonies, making the Witz one of the most enduring elements of living Maya spirituality.
summary: The Witz is the sacred mountain spirit in K'iche' Maya cosmology — the living consciousness of mountains that guards caves, grants visions, and connects the underworld to the heavens.
fun_fact: In K'iche' Maya, the word for 'throne' and 'mountain' are the same word: 'witz.' Every Maya king literally sat upon a mountain — a stone throne carved to resemble the sacred Witz.
seo_title: Witz – Mountain Spirit of Maya Cosmology
seo_description: The sacred mountain spirit in K'iche' Maya cosmology — the living consciousness of mountains guarding caves and connecting worlds.
source: Schele, Linda and David Freidel. 'A Forest of Kings: The Untold Story of the Ancient Maya.' William Morrow, 1990. Christenson, Allen J. 'Popol Vuh: Sacred Book of the Quiché Maya People.' Tulane University, 2007.

name: Ix Chel
description: Ix Chel is the Maya goddess of the moon, medicine, weaving, and childbirth. She is one of the most important and complex deities in the Maya pantheon. As a young woman, she is the beautiful Moon Maiden who aids lovers and heals the sick. As an old woman (Chak Chel), she is the Terrible Goddess who sends floods and disease. She is depicted with a serpent headdress, a weaving tool in her hand, and a乌龟 shell on her back. The island of Isla Mujeres off the Yucatán coast was her most sacred temple site. In Guatemala, she is particularly venerated in the Lake Atitlán region and by midwives.
appearance: As the young Ix Chel: a beautiful woman with a crescent moon on her forehead, wearing a jade necklace and a white huipil, holding a weaving baton. Her skin shimmers like moonlight. As Chak Chel (old woman): a wrinkled figure with clawed hands, a serpent crown, and a乌龟 shell on her back. Blood drips from her hands. She carries a broken weaving implement.
behavior: As the young Moon Maiden, she helps women in labor, guides the moon across the sky, andweaves the fabric of fate. As the old goddess, she overturns water vessels to cause floods, sends diseases to punish the unworthy, and weaves destruction during eclipses. She controls the tides and the cycles of women's bodies. She is served by owls and jaguars.
habitat: The moon itself. On earth, her sacred sites include Isla Mujeres, the cenotes (sacred wells) of the Yucatán, and Lake Atitlán in Guatemala. Midwives' clinics and weaving houses are her earthly domains.
cultural_significance: Ix Chel is the most important goddess in Maya tradition and remains actively venerated. She embodies the Maya understanding of feminine power — creative and destructive, healing and dangerous. Her association with weaving connects her to the fundamental Maya metaphor of reality as a woven fabric. Midwives invoke her before every birth. The annual pilgrimage to Isla Mujeres in her honor continues to this day.
summary: Ix Chel is the Maya goddess of the moon, medicine, weaving, and childbirth — a dual-natured deity who is both the beautiful Moon Maiden and the destructive Chak Chel.
fun_fact: The Maya word for 'weaving' and 'destiny' are the same root. When Ix Chel weaves, she is literally weaving the fate of the world — and when she unravels her cloth, she can end it.
seo_title: Ix Chel – Maya Moon Goddess of Guatemala
seo_description: Maya goddess of the moon, medicine, weaving, and childbirth — both the beautiful Moon Maiden and the destructive Chak Chel.
source: Miller, Mary Ellen. 'Maya Art and Architecture.' Thames & Hudson, 1999. Read, Kay Almere. 'Handbook of Mesoamerican Mythology.' ABC-CLIO, 2000.
